start: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: Fiona Hartley. Consultant anaesthetist, and the Trust's Caldicott Guardian.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: I speak for patients' confidentiality. When their records are at risk, I want to know who's telling them, and when.
patient_data: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: We hold records for over half a million patients. Diagnoses, medicines, next of kin.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: The ICO will ask whether it was taken, or only locked.

c-0: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: Then we can't prove it wasn't taken, and the ransom note says it was. We report it as possible theft.
c-1: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: In time. Forensics may take weeks, and the ICO deadline won't wait for it.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: So we report possible theft now, and if forensics clears it, we say so later.
c-2: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: That's the safe position. Assume it was taken, report promptly, and update as the facts come in.

disclosure_law: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: Article 33. We tell the ICO within seventy-two hours of becoming aware. Not of knowing everything.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: Article 34 is the patients. If a breach is likely to put them at high risk, we tell them directly. Health records usually meet that bar.
disclosure_choices: ^What if we miss the ICO deadline?

c-0: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: For a late notification, up to eight point seven million pounds, or two per cent of turnover.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: For a public body the ICO is more likely to issue a reprimand, and publish it. That's what the Board fears.
c-1: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: NHS England, under the NIS rules. Helen reported to them last night. The NCSC is voluntary, but worth it.

ico_timing: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: Then she's being careful in the wrong place. The seventy-two hours run from awareness, contained or not.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: The report can say what we're about to do, and the rest can follow in phases. Tell her I said so, and the DPO will say the same.
isolation_concern: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: Ward 7 lost the EHR last night. Every other ward can still read the vendor's cloud copy: allergies, drug charts.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: Cut the link and they lose it too. A wristband says penicillin. It won't tell you what the patient's had today.
isolation_choices: ^Then every ward prints its allergy and drug lists first, and pharmacy checks by phone.
^The attacker's still in. We isolate now and catch up.
^Can we leave the clinical link up and cut the rest?

c-0: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: Then I'll support it. The printouts and pharmacy cover most of it. What's left, I can live with, and it goes on the log with my name.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: It isn't free. The print run takes the best part of an hour, and pharmacy will have to hold discharges to staff the phones.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: I'll get Helen to send the print order out now.
c-1: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: That may be right. Then it's a risk you're accepting, not one you've removed. Write it down, and say who owns it.
c-2: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: Ask Ravi, but I suspect the link the attacker used is the one the wards use. That's rather the problem.

patient_disclosure_talk: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: There's one decision I have to recommend to the Board, and I'd like your view. When do we tell patients?
^Dr Fiona Hartley: The note threatens to publish records. Forensics won't know what was taken for weeks.
^Now. Write to them and say what we know.

c-0: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: I agree. It's Article 34, and it's honest. If the records leak, they'll have heard it from us first.
c-1: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: That's tidier for us. If the records turn up online first, they'll hear it from a journalist.
c-2: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: That puts our embarrassment ahead of their risk. Article 34 asks about the risk to them.

b: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: And anyone harmed today is owed more than a letter. Duty of candour: we tell them, or their family, in person.

candour: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: The truth, in person, as soon as we can. That's the duty of candour. We say what happened, and we say sorry.

b: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: And Ms Okafor's pump is quarantined and reported to the MHRA. A device involved in a death always is.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: Helen's sent it, late. Now the reasons for the delay matter as much as the report.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: Helen's sent the ICO report before the isolation. Good.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: Helen tells me the ICO report has gone. Good. We're inside the window.

deadline_missed: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: The seventy-two hours have passed, and the ICO hasn't heard from us.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: We'll have to explain the delay in the notification. The ICO will look at that as hard as at the breach.

c-0: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: We can, and we must. Write down what delayed us and who decided.
c-1: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: The ICO tablet on the conference table has been counting down all morning. Next time, look at it.

ncsc_advisory: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: I would. They've seen this group before, and they'll warn other trusts. Ask Helen.
hub: ^What do we owe anyone who was harmed today?
^Helen wants this contained before she tells the ICO.
^What worries you about isolating the network?
^What do we have to tell the ICO, and when?

b: ^Dr Fiona Hartley: The deadline's gone. Make sure Helen sends it today, with the reasons for the delay.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: It went late. Now we explain why, in writing.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: The ICO has its first report. Keep the updates coming.
^Dr Fiona Hartley: The ICO clock is running. Don't let it run out.
